en: (No. 5295) (Title: Commentary on the Kātyāyanī Tantra) (The Illuminator of Mantra Exegesis)
(Author: Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha) (Folio 14) (Subject: Tantra)

Oṃ. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ. I bow to that mountain-born Pārvatī, the slender creeper who, by her power, became the mother and grandmother of Acala, Girīśa, and Giriśa, and the great-grandmother of all. (1) May those who are connoisseurs of the essence of the crest-jewels of the Vedas and who are intensely eager for the experience of the sweetness of the nectar of the lips of the beloved of the Lord of Heaven be blessed. (2) But for us, may that [Pārvatī], whose form dwells within the caves of the Snowy Mountain, long bring wonder to the eyes of the gods.

(3) "Do not strike this body"—this is the external meaning; "Do not swallow this one born of Menā"—that is, the form of Umā—this is the hidden meaning. I take refuge in my mother, the illustrious Lakṣmavatī, the supreme teacher Lakṣmī; and in my father, named Raṅganātha, the supreme teacher. (4) I, Nīlakaṇṭha by name, whose surname is Śaiva, [composed this] within the *Kātyāyanītantra*, which divides the *Saptaśatī* into seven hundred mantras. (5) In the midst of the *Kātyāyanītantra*...

He composes this commentary, which is like a milch-cow for the calves, for the gratification of Śiva and Śivā and for the joy of the people. (6) Now, this *Saptaśatī* hymn—beginning with "Mārkaṇḍeya said" and ending with "Sāvarṇi will be the Manu"—consisting of thirteen chapters and contained within the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, is a granter of all desires. Though composed by someone [else], it is indeed the very mouth of the Veda. As it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśvarī Saṃhitā*: "The Veda is the cow; that which is beginningless is its calf, and the *Saptaśatī* is that [calf]."

It is stated in the *Merutantra* as well: "The entire reality of the *Saptaśatī* is indeed hidden within the Vedas; Śrī Hari knows three-quarters of it, Prajāpati knows half, Vyāsa knows a fourth part, and other people know but a ten-millionth part. Because it was revealed by Vyāsa, there is a worldly convention that it is "composed by Vyāsa" (*vyāsakṛta*). Furthermore, in the *Rudrayāmala*: "There exists a most secret majesty of the Goddess (*Devīmāhātmya*) which bestows all perfections, consisting of the words, meanings, and verses of the *Saptaśatī*."

It is auspicious in its nature, characterized by distinctions, yet ultimately it is the direct locus of the glory of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*); through the intended meaning (*tātparya-gati*), that entire work is the locus of non-dual consciousness.

In this regard, this hymn has two names: *Saptashatī* and *Saptashatī*. Regarding the etymology of these, the *Merutantra* states: "In the first [chapter] concerning the life-story of Saptashatī, the sage is Padmaja (Brahmā), the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, the deity is Mahākālī, the seed-syllable is Vāk (AIM), the principle (*tattva*) is Fire (Pāvaka), and its application is for the sake of Dharma and Artha."

There are ninety applications for killing and bewildering; here, for driving away (uccāṭana) and paralyzing (stambhana), there are two hundred applications. In the middle course of conduct, and likewise in the third course of conduct, there are considered to be various applications for creating enmity and subjugation (vaśya). Thus, seven hundred applications have been proclaimed here.
Therefore, it was called "Saptaśatī" (The Seven Hundred) by the wise Vyāsa. Furthermore, in the first of the seven Kalpas, [it begins with] "Mahāvidyā," etc., which is true.

The deities who arose as those to be worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Guru (Bṛhaspati), Śukra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the gods, and the enemies of the gods were praised here by Brahmā; therefore, it was proclaimed by Vyāsa as the *Saptaśatī*. Likewise, in the *Madhyama-carita*, the mantras of Lakṣmī, Lalitā, Kālī, Durgā, Gāyatrī, Arundhatī, and Sarasvatī are found; and likewise, the mantras of the seven Saptīs—Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sumukhī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bālā, and Kubjā—are present.

They were spoken in a concealed form; therefore, the name "Saptasatī" [is derived from] that. Likewise, in the third chapter, the seven beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Cāmuṇḍā, as well as Ānandā, Śākambharī, Bhīmā, Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmarī—these seven true ones are declared as the Saptasatī; thus, the name "Saptasatī" is clearly established in the Merutantra. In that regard, for the fire-oblation (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and the encapsulation (saṃpuṭīkaraṇa) with mantras, one must perform the oblation only after having divided the Saptasatī mantras [into their respective parts].
Based on the statement in the forthcoming *Kātyāyanītantra*— which says that [the recitation] must be performed with seven hundred mantras, otherwise it becomes fruitless—

it is necessary to have a division of this *Saptaśatī* hymn into seven hundred mantras; that division of mantras is stated in the *Kātyāyanītantra*, and it is here clarified through a commentary on the *Kātyāyanītantra*.

Īśvara said: "Mārkaṇḍeya uvāca adya" (Mārkaṇḍeya said today)—this is its meaning. The first mantra begins with "mārkaṇḍeya uvāca. Following that, it is joined with the second vowel, *ā* (ā-kāra). It is joined with the first letter of *vyoma*, which is *ha*; thus, *sā* is established. Starting from that, there are eighteen verses ending with the two syllables "nṛpam"; such is the number of those [verses] consisting of ślokas.

The meaning is that they constitute mantras. In this regard, although there are seven ślokas prior to the half-verse beginning with "Then Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun," and ending with "the Vaiśya, bowed down with humility, replied to the king" (which is itself a half-verse), it should be understood that by accepting only the final half-verse as a mantra, the designation "śloka" is applied to the entire verse according to the *chatrinyāya* (the logic of the umbrella-bearer). Thus, together with the first mantra...

Īśvara said: Mārkaṇḍeya said: First is the mantra consisting of verses; then, beginning with the syllable *vyo* and joined with the second vowel (*u*), ending with the word *nṛpa*, there are eighteen mantras, O beloved. Then follows the speech of the Vaiśya, which consists of verses beginning with *vyo* and ending with *saṃvama*.

These [first] nineteen mantras are complete; "the speech of the Vaiśya" means that there is one mantra consisting of the words "the Vaiśya said. Then, after that, starting from the letter *ha* (which is the first of the sky, etc.)—that is, starting from the letter *sa* (since the ablative case is used with the elision of the verbal suffix *lyap*)—there are four verses (by implication), and the remainder is that they constitute five mantras, because there are exactly four verses up to that point. Now, regarding these four verses...

If it is asked how there are five mantras, it is because the status of mantra is accepted for the first half-portion of the verse; as it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśī-saṃhitā*: "This [first] half-verse is my *samādhi-mantra*, and the meaning is the mantra; thus, together with the final half-verse, the five mantras are proclaimed. (2)

The phrase "the king’s speech" (*nṛpasyoktiḥ*) means "the king said," and the remainder is that it becomes a single mantra. The letter at the end (*māntavarṇaḥ*)—meaning the letter *ya*, which ends in the letter *m*—is joined with the letter *e*; by that, the mantra *yai* is established at the beginning. Furthermore, the letter *sa* is joined with a bindu (*bindusaṃyuktaḥ*) at the end (*ante*); these two mantras are thus formed. The intention is that in the verse beginning with *yair nirastaḥ*, one should divide it into two parts to produce these two mantras. (3) Then the Vaiśya spoke; thus [ends] the Vaiśya.

"He spoke"—the meaning is that he addressed them as a single mantra. Among the vowels, the eleventh vowel is *e* (svarekāra). Furthermore, at the beginning of the group starting with *s*, there is the seed-syllable of fire, which is *ra*. How is it? It is "joined with the bindu" (*binduyukta*). By that [seed-syllable], it is "measured" (*ramita*); the meaning is that the fivefold mantra should have such a form at its end. Here too, it is exactly as previously stated: the King’s utterance begins with the letter *ma* joined with the vowel *e*, and the letter *sa* joined with the bindu is at the end of the mantra.

Such is the opinion of the two [sages]. Then the Vaiśya said: "The seed-syllable of Fire (*ra*) joined with the moon (*u*), followed by the five *ātman* syllables, beginning with the eleventh vowel (*au*)—this constitutes the first mantra. Then there is one [syllable], and thereafter three mantras should follow: the letter *ta*, joined with the earth-vowel (*u*) and the vowel of the world (*o*), ending with the final syllable of Varuṇa (*va*). Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Then there shall be three mantras. [He continued:
"The letter *ta*, joined with the earth-vowel (*u*) and the vowel of the world (*o*), and ending with the final syllable of Varuṇa (*va*). (5)
From "tyārabhya" up to "niṣṭhuram," there are four verses;

according to the aforementioned principle, it should be understood that these constitute five mantras by including the first half-verse and the final half-verse along with the three intermediate verses. (4) "Mārkaṇḍeya uvāca" and "caikitāyana mārkaṇḍeya uvāca" constitute one mantra. Then, the one whose initial letter is "tādi" (beginning with *ta*) and whose final letter is "takāra" (the letter *ta*), [and] whose vowel is "bhuvanasvara" (the vowel *o*).

Thus, having joined [the parts] with the syllable *oṃ* at the end, there should be a triad of mantras of this kind. Here too, it should be understood that the status of being a triad of mantras is established by separating the final half-verses of the two half-verses beginning with "tatastau" and ending with "pārthivau," and joining them with a single intermediate verse. As it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśī-saṃhitā*:
"Then those two half-verses would constitute this [mantra]. (5)

The King said—meaning "the King said" constitutes one mantra. Then, those mantras which begin with the letter *bha* and end with the letter *ya* are considered to be six mantras; this is the meaning. Here too, it should be understood that they constitute six mantras by separating the first and last halves. As for the final half-verse, its status as a mantra should be understood from the statement in the *Haragaurī Tantra*: "O Dear One, those mantras which end with 'said' (*uvāca*) are of the nature of half-mantras. Now...

"Vāceti"—immediately thereafter, "the sage said," meaning this constitutes one mantra. Following that, beginning with "jñānamasti" (knowledge exists), [the text continues]. Then, "sarveśvareśvarī" (the Sovereign of all sovereigns); "mārkaṇḍeya uvāca" (Mārkaṇḍeya said)—this would be three mantras. Then the syllable beginning with 'ta', joined with the vowel of the world (u) and ending with the letter of Varuṇa (va)—[this is] the fifth. "Rājo vāceti" (The King said)—these six auspicious mantras, O fair-faced one, begin with 'ā' and end with 'ā'. Then, beginning with "ṛṣirjñānamasti" (The sage said, knowledge exists), O Pārvatī—[he] spoke. (6) Sa.

The twelve mantras are proclaimed as ending with the words "rveśvareśvarī. The King said: "O Lord, O best among the knowers, this triad of mantras is well-known at the beginning and the end. (7) Afterwards, the Sage said: "She is eternally the Mistress of the World; the eighth mantra is at the end. (8) The twelve mantras are proclaimed as ending with [the word] "tyantā"; the first half and the ten verses in the middle, together with the final half, are combined according to the previous method.

The twelve mantras are to be known as follows: "The King said" (*rājovāca*) occurs once; then, at the beginning with "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) and at the end with "O Knower of the Supreme" (*vidā vara*), there are two such verses, which—consisting of the first half of the first verse, the middle of the second, and the final half of the third—constitute three mantras according to the previously established rule.
After that, "The Seer said" (*ṛṣiruvāca*) occurs once; then, beginning with "Eternally indeed she [is] the world" (*nityaiva sā jagat*) and ending with "The Lord" (*prabhuḥ*), there are seven verses.
The meaning is that among those [mantras], the first half-verse, the six intermediate verses, and the eighth mantra consisting of half a verse—[these constitute the group]. (8)
The meaning is as follows: "Then Brahmā said" and "Thus Brahmā said" constitute one mantra. Then, from "O great Asuras beginning with Svāhā" up to the end, there are fourteen verses;
according to the previously established method, these consist of fifteen mantras, comprising the first half-verse, the middle thirteen verses, and the final half-verse.
(9) Regarding "The Seer thus": "The Seer said" constitutes one mantra. The six verses beginning with "Thus praised" and ending with "Keśava" are the first [set].

The meaning is that there are seven mantras in addition to the five verses in the middle of the *ṛk* [hymn]. Then follows the speech of the Blessed One, beginning with "The Blessed One said" (*bhagavānuvāca*). Or else, it begins with "Then Brahmā said" (*atha brahmovāca*), followed by "Then you, Svāhā, you, Svadhā, and these others—the great Asuras—these are considered the final five mantras, O beloved" (9). When the *ṛṣi* had thus offered praise, those [mantras] beginning with *Tat* and ending with Keśava became unified; then the Blessed One...

The two mantras "ktiḥ syāt" and "bhavetām" are for the two earths; with the words "ayārṣivīcitābhyām," there are these two mantras for Śiva; and the two mantras beginning with "ṛṣyuktiśca tatheti" should likewise be recited.
Regarding the phrase "What would be the mantra?", the meaning is that there are two mantras in the two sections of the verse beginning with "May he be pleased today" (10). Then, regarding "the seer":
one mantra is "The seer said," and the two mantras beginning with "Deceived by the two" constitute this pair of mantras.

This mantra was spoken by the two who were deceived; furthermore, there is the "Half-Mantra" *Jalapradītihara-gaurī-tantra-ardhamantra*, the single verse-mantra of Vasiṣṭha, and the pair of mantras consisting of the two verses beginning with "The Ṛṣis said" (*ṛṣaya ūcuḥ*) and "Having said 'So be it'" (*tathety uktvā*), etc.; these are not included here.
There is a half-verse mantra.

[Question: Are not all the verses in this chapter composed of four lines? To that he replies: "All the verses. This means that in this first chapter, all the verses are considered to be seventy-eight, consisting of four lines each; however, the mantras that are half-verses in the middle are to be understood according to the manner previously stated.
Twenty-four [mantras] are declared; this itself is the indicator that in the middle there are half-mantras. (12) He said: "How many end with 'uvāca'? To that he replied:

"All the verses in this chapter are considered to be seventy-eight; however, the half-verses and mantras in the middle are declared to be twenty-four. (12) Among those, it should be understood that the mantras end with 'uvāca'.
The oblations should be known collectively as numbering one hundred and four (104), equal to the number of worlds (bhuvana).

Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the division of the Saptashati mantras according to the Kātyāyanī Tantra. [The Seer said: "Ending with 'cāntāḥ'"; [The King said: "Beginning with 'rājovāca' and so forth"—these mantras are equal in number to the worlds, amounting to fourteen. Let it be so.

Regarding the question of how many [offerings] are produced by their combination, he says: "by their combination. The meaning of this is quite clear. (13) Thus ends the twentieth chapter (20) in the commentary on the Kātyāyanīya Tantra.

Īśvara said: "In the second [chapter], the Sage spoke"—this means that in the second chapter, the mantra "the Sage spoke" occurs for the first time. Together with those, by adding sixty-eight verses, sixty-nine oblations (*āhuti*) are produced; thus it results in "sixty-nine. The singular number in the word *āhuti* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). Then, in the third chapter, regarding the two teachers in the form of the Guru, O Pārvatī, there is one mantra: "the Sage spoke" (1). Following that, thirty-five verses...
Īśvara said: "The seer spoke" and so forth constitutes ninety-six oblations in sequence;

then, in the third [section], one should meditate on "the seer spoke," O Teacher (deśika). Thus, O fair-faced one, thirty-five mantras are to be known from the verses; at the end of each mantra, the verse beginning with "the Goddess spoke" [is added].
Then follows the utterance of the Ṛṣi: "Kastaṃtaḥparam" (2). Then there are five verses and eternal mantras;

thus, the oblations there amount to forty-four (3). In the fourth sequence, O Goddess, is the utterance of the Ṛṣi consisting of twenty-six [verses]; then again, likewise, the utterance of the Ṛṣi consists of two verses.
The two are of the nature of mantras. (4)

The meaning is that "rūpamantrāḥ" refers to the mantras [of form]. Then, "the Goddess said" (*devy uvāca*) constitutes one mantra; at the end of that, "one mantra" means a single verse consisting of a single *śloka*.

(2) The utterance of the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is "the Seer said" (*ṛṣir uvāca*), which is one mantra; furthermore, five verses mean five mantras. In this manner, there are forty oblations (*āhuti*) together with the four [initial ones]. (3) Regarding the phrase "in the fourth": in the fourth chapter, the utterance of the Seer is the mantra "the Seer said" (*ṛṣir uvāca*); after that, six... [text ends]
The mantras consisting of twenty ślokas, followed by one mantra beginning with "the sage spoke again" (ṛṣir uvāca), and then two further ślokas in the form of mantras— (4).

In the midst of that, when praised thus by the gods, this mantra becomes extremely secret and exceedingly purifying; Śiva alone knows this secret, and it is not within the range of our vision. Then the Goddess spoke—this is one mantra. Then [the phrase] "let [it] be chosen" refers to the mantra consisting of sixteen syllables and forming half a verse. (5) Regarding "the gods said"—this is one mantra. Having uttered that mantra, one should say, "Everything has been accomplished by the Blessed Lady. To the question of how far one should say this, he states: "the mantra..."

The word *yam* consists of twelve syllables; when joined with the subsequent [syllables], it becomes enriched by one hundred syllables, totaling one hundred and twelve syllables—that is to say, consisting of three and a half verses. This means that up to that extent, it is a single mantra. This prescription for it being a single mantra is intended solely for the purpose of fulfilling specific desires through the recitation of the mantra alone. Thus, having praised it as "this mantra is extremely secret and very purifying," the Goddess said: "Let this sixteen-syllable mantra be chosen. (5) The Devas...
Then they said, "O Blessed One, please tell us [the mantra]. This mantra consists of one hundred and twelve syllables.

Furthermore, it has been stated elsewhere that what is taught as being supreme is indeed the most excellent; this was mentioned in passing to indicate that, but not with the intention that a single oblation should be offered with a mantra consisting of three and a half verses, for that would contradict the number of oblations to be performed at the end of the chapter. Therefore, in this case as well, the mantra should be divided into sections before performing the homa. In that regard...

Since it is stated in the *Vaneśī-saṃhitā* that "O Bhagavatī, this half-verse is remembered as the fulfiller of all desires," one should understand that there is one mantra consisting of a half-verse beginning with "Whatever is done by the Bhagavatī," followed by three mantras consisting of three verses each. (6)

The meaning is as follows: "Then the sage spoke" (*tato rṣir uvāca*) and "the sage spoke" (*ṛṣir uvāca*) constitute a single mantra. At the end of each [section], there are four verses beginning with *tadante* and *prasādinā*; these also become mantras at their respective ends. (7) He sums up the total number of mantras for the entire chapter: "There are thirty-five verses. This means that the mantras consist of thirty-five verses, which are to be understood according to the sense of the five [sections] ending with the word *uvāca*. In that very context, by combining two half-mantras, there are forty-two mantras, being forty plus two. Thus...
Then the Ṛṣi said: "The four verses beginning with 'atitiprāsādita' are the mantras; those [verses] are the end.
There are seven verses in the fourth chapter, thirty-five."
O Śatyareśvarī, by means of these two half-mantras, there are again forty-two;
thus, for the middle narrative,
there are one hundred and fifty-five mantras.
(9) Due to the non-difference from Mahālakṣmī. (8) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Kātyāyanī Tantra.
(9) It combines the number of the middle narrative; thus, "of the middle narrative" is clear. (9) The first hundred, and after that, increased by five—five [hundred].
This is the meaning. (155) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Kātyāyanī-tantra-prakāśa*. (21) || || ||

In the fifth chapter, the phrase "the seer said" (*ṛṣiruvāca*) constitutes one mantra. Then, beginning with "purā" and ending with "pratuṣṭuvuḥ," there are six mantras in the form of verses; this is the meaning. Following that, "the gods said" (*devā ūcuḥ*) is one mantra. (1) Regarding the section beginning with "namo devyai": starting from "namo devyai" and ending with "vinamramūrtibhiḥ," there are thirty verses; within that, the passage beginning with "viṣṇumāyā-śabditā" is of the nature of a delusion (*bhrānti*).

The meaning is that there are twenty-one mantras composed of this final phrase, "ṇasaṃsthitā," which, when divided into three sections, become sixty-three. (2) If one asks how the three sections are to be made, he says: "By the numbers obtained from the word 'avatārau,' the mantras are to be made separately into three sections. The Sage said: "In ancient times, six mantras in the form of verses praised Viṣṇu’s Māyā; thereafter those gods spoke [as follows]: (1) 'Namo...'"

There are thirty verses beginning with "vyādinaḥ" [for Viṣṇu], and sixty-three verses beginning with "viṣṇumāyā" for the deities whose forms are bowed in devotion; these constitute the sixty-three mantras for the individual incarnations, and their offering consists of sixty-three oblations.

In that regard, the letter *ā* signifies the vowel class (*ā-varga*), by which the number sixteen is indicated; the letter *va*, according to the convention of Vararuci, signifies the number four. Combined, these constitute the first section consisting of twenty syllables, beginning with *viṣṇu-mapi-tyā-di-na-mas-ta-syai-pa-ry-aṃ-taṃ*. Then, in the word *tāre*, the letter *ta* signifies the number six, and the letter *ra*...

When combined with the number two, this second section consists of eight syllables. Although, according to the sequence of this text, this is obtained as the second section, nevertheless, [it is said]: "The syllable *vedā* (four) is not pleasing to Mahālakṣmī in the middle; however, in the *Lakṣmīsūkta*, O Śivā, this very [syllable] is expressed by the word *tā*.

From the statement in the thirty-third chapter, the third section (*khaṇḍa*) is to be understood. "Salutation to her" (*namas tasyai*) constitutes the second section. Thus, for each verse, three mantras are produced; the meaning is that sixty-three oblations (*āhuti*) are to be known as the offerings for these. (3) When the triad of mantras has been obtained from the root text and other tantras, something was whispered by someone in the *Guptavatī*: "The Goddess who is designated as 'Viṣṇumāyā' among all beings—to her [be] salutation, salutation, salutation. This twenty-four-syllable mantra is to be recited three times.
"One [verse] beginning with 'the presiding deity of the senses' constitutes another single verse.

O Goddess of the Suras, one should likewise offer three oblations with the mantra in the form of *cit* (*citi*). Thus, O Goddess of the Suras, those eighty mantras are together with the preceding ones. (3–4)

One should ask: "By which Guru was it taught that there are three Ācārya-oblations? Thus, it is established that the first mantra consists of twenty syllables, the second of four syllables, and the third of eight syllables. [The phrase] "the presiding deity of the senses" refers to this mantra consisting of a single verse.

(3) Regarding the words "in the form of consciousness" (*citirūpeṇa*), the meaning is that one should perform the three oblations with the mantra "by whom all this is pervaded" (*yayā kṛtsnaṃ*) according to the reasoning previously stated. Such are the mantras.
Thus, by combining the sixty-seven mantras with the thirteen mantras beginning with "iti viṣṇumāyā," the meaning is that there are eighty mantras in total according to the method described.

(4) Furthermore, it should be understood that the two previously mentioned "uvāca" mantras are combined to complete the count of eighty; thus, the pair beginning with "tat" and ending with "stute" is praised by the Asuras.

The meaning is that there are two mantras beginning with *ṛtyādi*. "The Seer said" (*ṛṣiruvāca*) is one mantra. From "Thus, [the gods] endowed with praise and so forth" (*evaṃstavādiyuktānām*) up to "Why is it not accepted by you? (*tvayā kasmān na gṛhyate*), there are seventeen mantras; this is the meaning. (5) "The Seer said" (*ṛṣiruvāca*) is one mantra. Then, following "Indeed, having heard those words with certainty" (*tato vai niścayena niśamya*), there are three mantras consisting of the three verses beginning with "O Śumbha" (*śumbhe*); these are proclaimed as the "pure varieties" (*śuddhabheda*). The term "pure variety" (*śuddhabheda*) is an adjective used as a qualifier in the sense of being an embellishment. (6) Now, "O Messenger" (*atha dūte*) and "The Messenger said" (*dūtīvāca*) is one [mantra].

There, the sage spoke this pair of verses beginning with "tatrastuta": "Why are these seventeen mantras not accepted by you, even though they are joined with such praises? Thus, through these three—the sage’s speech, the word "niśam" (having heard), and so forth—the mantras are proclaimed as being of the pure division (*śuddhabheda*). Then the messenger spoke, beginning with "iti deva daityeśvara"; thereafter, the sage again spoke the nine mantras beginning with "iti". And with the single mantra beginning with "ityukta," the Goddess Sarasvatī spoke here.

Then there are four verses according to the division of mantras. (8) Then [the verse] beginning with "The messenger said" (*atha dūtīvāca*) is one; "O Gaurī, will you come? (*māgamiṣyasi*) is another; and thereafter the goddess spoke four mantras numbering that same amount. (9) The mantras beginning with "O Goddess, O Lord of Daityas" (*devi daityeśvara*) and so forth are nine mantras. "The Seer said" (*ṛṣir uvāca*) is one mantra. (7) Regarding the passage beginning with "Thus she was addressed" (*ity uktā sā tadā devī*): [she was addressed thus].
The meaning is that by this single verse alone, Sarasvatī is attained here; the intention is that "this mantra bestows the state of Sarasvatī. Then, "the Goddess said" constitutes one mantra.

Following that, there are four verses which are mantras. (8) Now, "the messenger said": "the messenger said" constitutes one mantra. There are four mantras ending with "O Gaurī, will you come? [said by] the Goddess. (99)

"Thus" (*evam*) means: beginning with "O powerful Śumbha" (*evametad balī śumbha*) and ending with "let him do this" (*yad ittham*), there are these two mantras. In this manner, all those verses are nine in number. Furthermore, there are nine *aṅga-mantras* (limb-mantras). Here, the word *nava* (nine) indicates the number seven by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), in accordance with the number to be stated later. As for the word *aṅga*, it refers to the *ārambha-mantras* (initiatory mantras), according to the lexicon which states: "The word *aṅga* is proclaimed [to mean] a limb of the body, as well as a beginning (*ārambha*). Thus, the meaning is that they are the initiatory mantras. And the Sage said to the Goddess...

"May the powerful Śumbha act accordingly"—these two mantras, along with the mantras forming the verses and those [verses] themselves, amount to one hundred and twenty-nine mantra-forms. (10) "The Seer said"—having heard this, four verses were uttered. (11) Again, "The Seer said"—after being thus commanded by him, these three mantras were spoken; then follows "The Goddess said. (12-12-12)

The meaning is that all the mantras beginning with "vācā" and so forth, totaling forty-nine mantras in this chapter, when combined with the previously mentioned eighty mantras, result in one hundred and twenty-nine mantras. (10) Then, in the sixth chapter, regarding the statement "the Rishi said," there is one mantra consisting of the words "ṛṣir uvāca"; furthermore, four verses beginning with "iti ākarṇya" are declared to be mantras. (11) Again, regarding "the Rishi said," [there is] the Rishi...
"Ruvāca" is one mantra; by him [the Lord] being thus commanded, the three mantras beginning with "tataḥ śīghram" are proclaimed; "devyuvāca" is one mantra (12);
"daityeśvareṇa" is one mantra, meaning "sent by the lord of the Daityas"; then immediately after that, the mantra "ṛṣiruvāca" [is recited]; and then immediately after that...

At the end of the word *ityukta* (thus spoken), in the passage beginning with *sa abhyadhāvata* (he ran toward), there are twelve verses starting with that; through these twelve verses, offerings to twelve deities are made.

(13) He describes the initial offerings as "the twenty-four divisions"; this means that in the sixth chapter, there are offerings numbering twenty-four. (14) Then, in the seventh chapter, there is the "utterance of the Ṛṣi," which is one mantra beginning with *ṛṣir uvāca* (the Ṛṣi said); after that, [there is] the command (*ājñapta*).

The mantra sent by the lord of the Daityas is proclaimed; then, having said "So be it," the sage Artha ran after him. (13) These twelve verses beginning with this are proclaimed in the sixth chapter. Those offerings to the deities are of twenty-four varieties in sequence. (14) Beginning with "The sage’s speech was commanded," there are twenty-three [verses on] the Mothers. The sage said: those two have passed away; [this concludes] the division of the mantras.
In this sequence, O Goddess, twenty-seven oblations arise from the words; here, in these two chapters, Dhūmrākṣī is proclaimed [as the first], and so forth.
The meaning is that by his command, the Mothers numbering twenty-three, beginning with the Daityas and others, become the oblations. Ṛ.

"Śiruvāca" is one mantra; "tāvānītāvi" consists of two mantras. (15) "Saptaviṃśat" means, O Goddess, that all these aforementioned oblations amount to twenty-seven in number. The meaning here is that this pair of chapters must necessarily be recited by a devotee of the deity Dhūmrākṣī within these two chapters. (16)

Regarding the eighth chapter, beginning with "The sage said: 'And Caṇḍa was slain,'" there is one mantra consisting of the words "The sage said" (*ṛṣiruvāca*). From "And Caṇḍa was slain" until the end of the chapter, sixty-three oblations are prescribed. Among those, there is one oblation for the half-verse, while the others consist of full verses and number sixty-one.
Including the single oblation for "The sage said," there are thus sixty-three oblations in total. In that regard, the natural mantra consists of the verses.

In view of the requirement for a separation [of the mantra], it is appropriate that the status of *mantra* belongs only to the portion existing at the end, namely "hatamātṛgaṇā" (17). And the seer [is mentioned] with "ra ṛṣiścaṇḍe ca nihate," which concludes the chapter; sixty-three oblations are prescribed, as well as one half-oblation (17). The deities are proclaimed to be eight, beginning with Raktākṣī; the king [recites] "vicitram" and so forth.
Two verses have been cited [beginning with] "The sage became enraged" (*ṛṣiścakārakopaṃ hi*) and so forth;

they should be understood as thirty-seven in terms of the nature of the deity-mantras (18–19). There are forty-one oblations in the ninth [chapter]; O fair-faced one, listen to the secret of the goddess Bhairavī-Tārā (20).

The eight Śaktis—Brahmī and the others—who have emerged from the forehead of the Goddess Kṛtyā and possess red eyes, appear as deities in this chapter; the sense is that this chapter must be recited regularly by her worshippers. In the ninth chapter, regarding "O King, it is wonderful," there is one verse beginning with "The King said" (*rājovāca*), and two verses beginning with "It is wonderful" (*vicitram*); [these were composed] by the Seer (*ṛṣi*).
Beginning with "vāce" and "ekaśca kāraka upa," there are twenty-seven mantras in verse form. (19) All the oblations (*āhuti*) in this ninth chapter amount to forty-one;
the deity of this chapter is Bhairavī Tārā, as before. (20)

In the tenth chapter, "Ṛṣir niśumbham" constitutes one mantra, "Ṛṣir uvāca" [is another], and "Niśumbhaṃ nihataṃ" and so forth constitute two mantras; this is the meaning. Then, "Devī uvāca" is one mantra, and "Tata ekāivāham" and so forth are two unsurpassed mantras; this is the meaning. (21) Again, "Devī caikā" means that "Punar devī uvāca" is one mantra. Following that, together with the single mantra "Ahaṃ vibhūtyā," there are eight previously mentioned mantras.

The seer said, "They were accomplished," thus one [verse]; then there are twenty-two and a half mantras beginning with "Then it proceeded. Among those, the twenty-second verse consists of two mantras beginning with "The seer [saw] Niśumbha slain. Then there are two mantras beginning with "Then the Goddess. Or, by means of a single mantra beginning with "I am the unsurpassed one" (21), eight mantras are also cited beginning with "O Goddess. Then the seer [recited] twenty-two and a half verses beginning with "Then it proceeded" (22).
Therein, twenty-two *manus* are mentioned, and one is considered to be half a *manu*. In the tenth [chapter], they are seated upon lions, bearing tridents and nooses;
the principal ones have four arms, hold arrows and bows in their hands, and possess auspicious eyes. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Kātyāyanītantra*.
O auspicious one, the seer (*ṛṣi*) proclaimed by the Goddess in this *Hṛdaya* is the renowned Sumedhas; there are thirty-four verses, and the mantras are equal in number to those.
Which are remembered?

(1) "The fires born from the *rūpa-mantras* blaze forth"—this is one mantra at the end of the half-verse. It should be understood that in this entire chapter, there are thirty-two mantras. The tenth [mantra], beginning with "ityādi," is to be known as clear, as before. (22) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Kātyāyanī-tantra-prakāśa*. [The Seer is Su...]*

The meaning is as follows: "Medhātithi" is one mantra; "In the eleventh [chapter], the Ṛṣi said" is one mantra; and starting from "Devī uvāca" (the Goddess said), there are thirty-four verses, which constitute that many mantras. (1)

The mantra "tat iti" spoken by the Goddess is joined with the subsequent mantra "I am the giver of boons"; thus, two mantras are to be understood. (1) "The gods said" is one mantra, joined with the subsequent single mantra "the pacification of all afflictions"; thus, two mantras are established. (2) "The Goddess said" is one mantra;

thereafter, from "in the Vaivasvata interval" onwards, there are fourteen verses which constitute mantras. (3) Together with the five [preceding], these fifty oblations are [performed] with half-mantras.

Then, by means of a single mantra, the Goddess said, "I am the Giver of Boons, O Sovereign of the Gods. Then all the gods spoke [a verse] regarding the pacification of all afflictions (2). O Mistress of the Gods, the Goddess then spoke one verse; thereafter follow fourteen and a half verses beginning with "Having arrived in the Vaivasvata interval" (3). O Goddess, the total number of oblations is fifty-five.

Accompanied by Vaiṣṇavī, the deity here is indeed Vaiṣṇavī, whose vehicle is the great Garuḍa. (4) The goddess spoke these words to them with praises, and together with the half-verse beginning with "māṃ tadā dūre," there are twenty-eight forms.
The meaning is that they occur within this chapter. Furthermore, that half-verse, by implication, has Vaiṣṇavī as its deity;

it should be understood as before. (4) Regarding "the Goddess said": "the Goddess said" constitutes one mantra. Then, starting from "by these praises of mine" up to the end, "they flee from afar," together with that final [half-verse], there are twenty-eight mantras in the form of verses; thus they should be understood. (5)

Then the sage said: "Tataśca" and "Ṛṣiruvāca" constitute one mantra. Having been addressed with "Tat," that Blessed Lady, beginning from the first verse and including the first half-verse, [performs] as many oblations as there are verses; such is the meaning. This is stated in the *Kātyāyanītantra*: "The mantra ending in 'ityuktā' is a half-mantra; through recitation, it bestows valor. (6) He describes the oblations for all the chapters: "In this way," etc., is clear. Then, in the thirteenth [chapter], the sage said: "Ṛṣiruvāca."
And "ceti" is one mantra (7). "O King, this has been told to you"—beginning from "O King, this has been told to you" up to the final half-verse, there are three verses;
then the Seer said "iti," and starting from the first verse, including the half-verse and nine verses, the mantras are intended to be that many (6).
Thus, in the twelfth chapter, there are forty-one oblations. After that—
In the thirteenth chapter, the meaning is that the sage spoke;
[the passage beginning] "This has been told to you, O King," and so forth, for three and a half verses, is the speech of Mārkaṇḍeya, who said, "Manu [spoke]."
Thus urged by his words, (8).

"Manu" refers to three and a half verses, meaning the mantras consist of that many. "Mārkaṇḍeya uvāca" (Mārkaṇḍeya said) is one [verse]. "Iti tasya vaco ditaḥ" (Thus his speech was uttered)—here "ārṣaprayogaḥ" (Vedic usage) applies;

there is a word-split (*cheda*) as "āditaḥ" (from the beginning), meaning "first. "Having heard his speech" constitutes one mantra consisting of half a verse. Consequently, there are six verses, which consist of five and a half mantras. According to the principle that "one creates forms," the term "verse" (*śloka*) is applied even to a half-verse. Thus, it consists of five verses.
The meaning is that the six mantras are formed by combining the *pāda*-mantras with the *arthaśloka*-mantra (22.8).

"The Goddess said" is one mantra; "O King, that which is requested by you" is another. Regarding this, he states a specific point with one verse: the meaning is that by repeating this very verse multiple times, one becomes pleasing to the Blessed Goddess (*Śrībhagavatī*). Therefore, the intent is that one should not accept the status of being a half-mantra (*ardhamantra*) here. (9) Mārkaṇḍeya.

"One [verse] says 'He spoke,' then follows the first two mantras beginning with 'The king [requested] the kingdom'; one [verse] says 'The Goddess spoke. Here, by means of three short verses—meaning three verses consisting of few words—there are six oblations (*ṣaḍāhuti*); this is the meaning. Now, how can there be six oblations in three verses? To that he says: 'In this case, only the half-verses constitute six verses; then there would be the speech of the Goddess, O Supreme Lady, regarding that which is requested by you, O King, in the verse.'"
"Not by one alone is satisfaction brought about. Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Then he chose two [mantras]. The Goddess said:

"And again, by three very short verses alone—(10)—because these half-verses constitute mantras, there are six invocations here. Then, having given 'O Mārkaṇḍeya' and 'to those two,' (11) the two mantras were recited once more."
Ryasa-varni will be the twenty-ninth in number.

"An oblation is prescribed here because it is a mantra" (12.12); the meaning is that there are six oblations by means of six half-mantras. Then, "O Mārkaṇḍeya," and "Mārkaṇḍeya said"—this constitutes one [half-mantra].

Regarding the phrase "having uttered the mantra" (*maṃtraḥ iti datvā*): the meaning is that after having uttered the mantra consisting of the half-verse beginning with "then" (*tato... iti*), two mantras follow. The first mantra consists of the single verse beginning with "immediately thereafter, the two [sons] became hidden" (*punaranantaraṃ dvau maṃtrau bhūvāṃtarhitau sadyaḥ*). The second mantra consists of the half-verse beginning with "having obtained birth from the Sun" (*sūryāj janma samāsādya*). After reciting these two mantras, one should recite at the end the mantra consisting of a single quarter-verse beginning with "he shall become a Sāvarṇi Manu" (*sāvarṇir bhavitā manuḥ*). This is the remainder of the instruction. One should recite this to indicate the completion of the book, but there is no oblation (*āhuti*) for it.
The meaning is as stated in the Kātyāyanītantra: "Having given [the offering] with the half-mantra 'for the fulfillment of desired aims'.

(12) Thus, in the thirteenth chapter, the phrase "this" connects with what precedes, while "in the rites of *homa* and *tarpaṇa*" connects with what follows; [therein it says] "seven hundred mantras in the *homa*s and so forth."

The meaning is that [the mantra] should be recited. Therefore, according to one's desire, by the recitation of one, two, or three mantras, this rule regarding the number of mantras is understood; for example, in cases such as "When Durgā is remembered," it refers to the recitation and so forth of the mantras alone. For this very reason, it should be understood that starting from "It was performed by the Blessed Lady," there is one mantra consisting of thirty and a half verses which was previously spoken by the Blessed One. (13) Regarding "in the true tradition" (*satsampradāya*), it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśvarī-saṃhitā*: "This [is] seven..."

The Goddess Śatī is undoubtedly a blazing fire; she is well-protected for the sake of happiness, otherwise she causes the burning of the house. (14) Thus, O Daughter of the Mountain, in this thirteenth chapter concerning the rites of *homa* and libation (*tarpaṇa*), seven hundred [verses] have been declared.
(13) The mantra beginning with the letter *ma* and ending with the letter *nu* is extremely difficult to obtain; it must be known through the method of the true tradition (*satsaṃpradāya*) from me.
Otherwise, the mantra is fruitless; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Śrī-Kātyāyanī-Tantra. (23)

Although there exists an authoritative commentary that has attained the meaning of the secret essence of the *Tyāyanī-tantra* and which has been relied upon by all learned men of every land from the beginning of the Satya Yuga until the present day, those who speak like madmen have disregarded that commentary and prattled on in the *Cidguptavatī* manuscript as follows: they treat the half-verse "He then thought there... as a single mantra, and likewise they treat the two half-verses "What indeed [was] theirs? and "How indeed [was] theirs? as mantras, and similarly [they treat] "For their sake... [as such].

In the *Saptaśatī*, beginning with the verse "romīti dvāvardhaślokakau manū," confusion regarding the measurement of all the mantras has been created; likewise, other commentators have also caused confusion regarding all the mantras of the *Saptaśatī* by accepting that a mantra consists of half a verse in some initial verses, and in other cases, accepting that a mantra consists of half a verse in some middle verses. And because of that—
The thought arose in the Supreme Lord: "If people were to commit unrighteousness (*adharma*) in all their actions, what would be the destiny of such practitioners of unrighteousness?

Now, one might ask: "Is this 'mantra-ness' defined as the nature of protecting through reflection (*manana-trāṇa-rūpatva*)? If so, that would not be correct; since that [quality of protecting through reflection] exists in the *Brāhmaṇas* as well, the definition of mantra-ness would be over-extensive (*ativyāpta*).

Furthermore, if it is stated that "a mantra is that which expresses a prescribed meaning," then there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), because the mantra "He sacrifices the *kapinjala* birds while causing them distress" (*saṃtāpaka-piṃjalān ālabhate*) is of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).

If it is argued: "Do not say so; the authors of the Śāstras employ the term 'mantra' in this way, because the designation 'mantra' is a faultless definition," and this has been clarified by Jaimini in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, *Taccodakeṣu Mantrākhyā* (The name 'mantra' applies to those [words] which enjoin that [action]), and furthermore, there is even the usage of the term 'mantra' for Śiva in the *Saptaśatī-mantra*; [we reply: it may be so, yet according to Jaimini, "that which has a single purpose is a single sentence (*vākya*), provided it is expectant [of completion] when divided."

By the rule *syād iti*, the definition characterized by syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) has been stated; its meaning is this: that which is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) when divided and possesses a single meaning (*ekārtha*) when not divided, that is a single sentence. In that regard, if it were merely stated that "it is expectant when divided," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For example, in the mantra: *syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi ghṛtasya dhārayā suṣevaṃ kalpayāmi | tasmin sīdāmṛte pratitiṣṭha vrīhīṇāṃ medha sumanasyamānaḥ* (I prepare for you a pleasant seat; with a stream of ghee I fashion it as a comfortable resting place. Sit upon it, O immortal one, stand firm, O essence of rice, being well-disposed). Here, in this [mantra]...

When there is a division of the collection of words beginning with "smin" (in), in order to determine the meaning of the word *tat* which expresses the subject at hand, there exists a requirement for the preceding collection of words; to exclude that [ambiguity], it is stated that [the two parts] have "a single meaning. Indeed, in this case, there is a single meaning: the purpose of the first half-verse is the preparation of the seat (*sadana-karaṇa*), while the purpose of the second half-verse is the firm establishment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-pratiṣṭhāna*). [The terms used are: *syona* means "excellent" (*samīcīna*) and "well-served" (*suṣeva*, i.e., well-frequented or suitable); *medha-sāra* refers to the essence of the sacrificial cake.

In this context, the fact that two collections constitute two distinct sentences is established by both parties; this is what is excluded by the phrase "having a single meaning" (*ekārtham*). If one were to say merely "having a single meaning," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*): for instance, in the case of the two mantras, "May Bhaga divide you two" and "May Pūṣan divide you two," although these collections of words are distinct mantras, the object intended by them—the substance consisting of the act of division—is one and the same. To exclude such cases, it is stated that they must be "mutually expectant regarding the division" (*vibhāge sākāṅkṣam*).

Since the two properties—being a mantra and being syntactically connected with a single governing context (*adhikaraṇa*)—are co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he then reflected upon the search for such half-verses (*ardhaśloka*). He thought: "In that case, only those half-verses beginning with *tadā tatra* and so forth would be possible. This is incorrect, because the flaw of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is difficult to avoid; for even though they are mantras, mantras such as *huṃ phaṭ* lack syntactic connection (*ekavākyatva*) [with a governing context], and furthermore, within the Brāhmaṇa texts...

Even though it is a sentence, it lacks the status of a *mantra*; thus, while such grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) may exist in some instances, it is absent everywhere else. Furthermore, in the thirteenth chapter, by accepting six *mantras* consisting of three verses each—beginning with "O King, in a few days" (*svalpairahobhir nṛpate*)—the Lord does not accept a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for those [verses] which are mutually required. Moreover, since the previously cited statements provide a solution for all cases, [there is no need for further restriction].

Furthermore, because there would be no utility in accepting that as the cause, and because the contradiction with the forthcoming *kārikā* would be difficult to avoid, the wise should discern that my own explanation is indeed more sound. On this point, some who delight solely in systematic consistency (*anugama*) say this: "Of the five hundred and seventy-eight verses that exist in the *Saptaśatī*, among those verses of a certain number where there are mantras ending with 'uvāca' (he said), therein [the rule applies]..."

Since the division of the concluding mantras has been shown, it should be understood that the two half-verses forming the preceding and following portions of the concluding mantra constitute two separate mantras.

For example, in the first episode, within the eighteenth verse, there is the concluding mantra "The Vaiśya said" (*vaiśya uvāca*); therein, the two half-verses of the preceding and following portions constitute two mantras: the half-verse beginning with "He replied to him, 'O Vaiśya... (*taṃ vaiśyaṃ pratyuvāca*) is one mantra, and "The Vaiśya said" (*vaiśya uvāca*) is another mantra. This is the resolution (*samādhi*).

In the *Saptaśatī*, there is a pervasive presence of mantras consisting of half-verses (ardha-śloka) such as "mavaiśyo'ham" and so forth; wherever a half-verse occurs at the end of a chapter, it naturally falls [as a mantra], just as in the case of "jajvaluścāgnayaḥ śāntāḥ. Similarly, in the passage "hate tasmin mātṛgaṇo'nartad asṛṅmadoddhataḥ," one should understand that it consists of two mantras made up of half-verses. At the end of the first narrative (*caritra*), the mantra "ṛṣiruvāca" constitutes the mantra of the statement.

Since [the end of] a preceding verse and [the beginning of] a subsequent verse fall at the end and the start [of a line], and not in the middle of a verse, there is no status of two separate mantras for the first and second halves [of a verse].

Thus, in the *Saptaśatī*, the division into seven hundred mantras is established through this very method of following [the text], even without an external authority. And this method of following was demonstrated by the author of the hymn itself by treating the end of a verse containing "uvāca" as the conclusion of a mantra. To that we reply: this method of following is indeed true.
If what you have stated were not in contradiction with the words of the *Kātyāyanī-tantra*, that would indeed be difficult to maintain;

for, while there are four verses beginning with "In a few days, O King" (*svalpair ahobhir nṛpate*) in the thirteenth chapter in accordance with your interpretation, according to the *Kātyāyanī-tantra* there are six mantras. Consequently, the contradiction with the *Kātyāyanī-tantra* is indeed unavoidable, as I have stated.

Let those of wise intellect who delight in the path discern [the truth] therein; if those who are more learned accept that following by adhering to that sequence, then we too shall accept it, for we have no dogmatism. Thus, just as a swan extracts the essence, O scholars, having abandoned the non-essential, please accept the essential through your discrimination of the essential and the non-essential. Now, regarding this *Saptaśatī*...

The verses spoken by the ancients regarding the division of the mantras are now written down. Mārkaṇḍeya said—this is declared as the first mantra. Then there are seventeen mantras consisting of half-verses (1). The speech of the Vaiśya is one half-verse; after that, three mantras are recorded. "How so?"—this is also a half-verse; the mantra "The King said" (2) follows. Then there are two mantras consisting of two half-verses; immediately after that is the speech of the Vaiśya. Then a mantra consisting of a half-verse is proclaimed. A mantra consisting of a half-verse is proclaimed. A mantra consisting of a half-verse is proclaimed. That which consists of three verses is a *mantra*; what would be half of that? Then there is the word of Mārkaṇḍeya; thereafter, this half-verse would be a single *mantra* consisting of one verse.

(4) The half-mantra beginning with "upaviṣṭau" and likewise the half-mantra beginning with "rājovāca bhagavan" constitute a group of four verses. (5) The half-mantra beginning with "mamāsya" is the sage’s speech; following that, the half-mantra beginning with "jñānamasti" makes ten mantras.

Following that, "In this saṃsāra... is half a mantra; then the King spoke, and "O Blessed One... is another half-mantra. Then follows the Manu-verse consisting of a full śloka. (7) All of that is half [of the next]; then the Sage’s speech, "It is eternal," is one half-mantra. Thus six mantras have been declared. Then "Sleep... is half a mantra. (8) Brahmā spoke, and then there is another half; following that, there are thirteen [syllables]. Then "Awakening... is half a mantra, and after that is the Sage’s speech. (9) Thus ends "Having praised in this way..."

Then follow five mantra-halves; thereafter, the two [sages] spoke a half-mantra and the words of the Blessed One. (10) "Let this be the half"—thus there is a half, and what else? Then there is the half-verse of the Sage's speech, and after that, the Śloka-mantra. (11) Following that is the Sage's speech, and finally, two mantras are proclaimed.
Thus, in the first chapter, the number of mantras has been declared. (12) Thus ends the first chapter. In the second, there are eight [mantras] of the Sage's speech.

The third [section] is known as the six syllables (*ṣaḍakṣara*); the words of the Sage (*munivākya*) consist of thirty-five syllables (*aṇu*). Then there is one verse of the Goddess (*devīvākya*), followed by the words of the Sage;
then the gods said—this is the mantra consisting of a single verse, the words of Ambikā, and thirty-four syllables. (17) The final half-verse is declared to be the mantra;

in the twelfth [section], the speech of Ambikā consists of twenty-eight mantras, and likewise there is one half-offering (*ardhāhuti*). (18) Again, there is the Sage, then the half-verse, and nine verses.
In the thirteenth [chapter], there are eleven and a half oblations; the mantras consist of twelve verses. (19) With six utterances, twenty-nine [verses] have been proclaimed.

The nectar of the *kārikās* has been extracted from the ocean of Gauḍapāda’s commentary. (20) May all the wise drink it, for thereby the destruction of death occurs. Thus ends the *Kārikā-bali*.
